# SAIRN Open Work Index

**One place to see everything that is open across the whole platform.**
Last rebuilt: **2026-08-23**. Last updated: **2026-09-23** (SAIRNroofing `rf_*` re-audit opened and CLOSED; SAIRNfreedom's NEEDS-OUTSIDE-COUNSEL tax question filed here for the first time — it had lived only in a research doc's prose). Before that: **2026-09-05** (sd-data's anonymous 268-name disclosure closed and independently reviewed, five residual rows opened; SAIRNscape's `scpLd()` fixed, 7 silent loaders left; StoneDesk's public surface has no tables; SAIRNroofing's published-PIN row closed and re-verified live).

Before this file existed, open work lived in `SAIRN-BACKLOG.md`, in
`SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK.md`, in ~40 per-app handoffs, and in skill files — so real
items got missed and sessions sat idle while work existed. This is the index.
It does not replace those files; each row points back at the source of truth.

**Note, 2026-08-24:** `SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK.md` was split per session to stop the
recurring merge conflicts. Its historical entries are still there (unchanged),
but new active-work entries go in `SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK-hank.md`,
`SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK-cc.md`, `SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK-cody.md`, and
`SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK-fourth.md` (one per clone). **The next rebuild of this index
must read all four, not just the shared file.**

---

## How to use this in 30 seconds

1. Filter by **Owner** — `unassigned` rows are the ones a free session can take.
2. Skip anything whose **Blocked by** is not empty unless you can clear the block.
3. Do what **Next action** says. If it says *verify*, the row's status is a claim
   that has not been re-checked; verify before building on it.

**Every row is a claim, not a fact.** Same standard as a handoff: re-verify
before you act on one. Rows marked ⚠️ are ones this rebuild could not confirm.

**AN ITEM NUMBER IN A SESSION SUMMARY IS NOT A REGISTRY ENTRY.** Recorded
2026-09-14 after a fresh session was handed a work queue naming *"the item
40/41/43/44/45 cluster"* and spent time looking for the fifth. At that moment
`grep -rn "item 45"` over the whole repo returned **zero hits** — no row here,
nothing in `docs/MASTER-PLAN.md`, nothing in any `SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK-*.md`, and
**no `items.md` has ever existed anywhere in this tree** (still true; re-checked
2026-09-16). The number came from a summary of a prior session, which is
exactly the kind of claim the paragraph above says to re-verify. **This file is
the registry. If a number is not in it, the item does not exist** — say so and
move on rather than hunting for it.

**AND THE NOTE ITSELF WENT STALE INSIDE A DAY, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH
KEEPING.** It was written in the present tense — *"returns zero hits"* — about
a grep, and on 2026-09-15 CC built `tools/trend_alarm.py` under the number and
filed a real row for it (the traceability-headline/backlog divergence row
below). So the sentence that made this note checkable became false while the
note went on asserting it, and a reader running that grep today gets a dozen
hits and no way to tell which claim is out of date. Corrected 2026-09-16 rather
than deleted, because the correction is the lesson: **a standing note whose
evidence is a command output must say WHEN it was run, and this one did not.**
Same shape as instrument drift — nothing announced the day the sentence stopped
being true. **Item 45 now EXISTS**, as a registry row, because somebody did the
work and filed one; what remains true is that it did not exist when it was
handed to a session as though it did.

the harness&rsquo;s `localStorage.setItem` could not fail, so no arm could ever see it; it gained `failWrite`/`failRemove` and a `removeItem`. **Two harness stubs were missing for the same reason** (`sdStorageFailed`, `_sbSaveFailed` are only touched when a write really fails), and the first failing arm died on a ReferenceError that would have hidden every storage arm behind it | S |

| **Platform** | **The watchdog now DOES something, and the response was decided before the incident** | **BUILT 2026-09-14 (Fourth)** &mdash; `api/_lib/cron-response.js`, 55/55 arms in `api/cron-watchdog.test.js` | &mdash; | **SATISFIED 2026-09-17:** `SAIRN_OPS_EMAIL` is set and the running function can see it, verified live; `SAIRN_ESCALATION_EMAIL` is still unset and deliberately does not count as missing | **Item 55, built on item 54.** A detector that stops at detecting hands the decision to whoever happens to read the output, at the moment they read it, under whatever pressure they are under. `RESPONSE` is a TABLE: one row per status the watchdog can produce, written down before the incident. **RETRY IS NOT THE ANSWER TO EVERY STATUS, and the exclusions are the reasoning:** `NEVER_BEAT` is a job that has never once completed &mdash; a deploy or a schedule that was never wired, so re-invoking it fails the same way while making the log look like flapping. `PARTIAL` on alf-alerts means sends were REJECTED, so a retry re-sends: at best a duplicate medication alert to a facility, at worst hammering a provider already refusing. `UNDECLARED` means nothing is wrong with the job at all &mdash; the watchdog&rsquo;s own list is stale &mdash; and retrying somebody else&rsquo;s healthy job is not a response, it is an unrelated side effect. **ALERT STORMS ARE THE FAILURE MODE OF EVERY SYSTEM LIKE THIS.** A DEAD job is DEAD on every run; alerting hourly for a week is 168 identical emails and the reliable consequence is a filter rule, after which THE NEXT REAL ALERT IS INVISIBLE. So an alert fires on a STATUS CHANGE or after 6h of the same status, never otherwise &mdash; **and what was suppressed is REPORTED, because a suppression nobody can see is indistinguishable from a detector that stopped working.** Retry is once per detection, never in a loop. Its own write is `on_conflict=license_hash,costlog_id` — keyed, one row per cost-log entry, no removal verb. **A false EXEMPTION never appears anywhere to be argued with, which is why it outlived a false finding would have** — the same lesson the baseline's own header already records about `rf_claims` and the append-only reader. **The window was wrong in BOTH directions:** `sd_public_shop`'s own write sits at offset **+2499** and the matched string runs past 2500, so it missed **by one character** and sat in the queue as a false entry. **AND THE FIX IS NOT A BIGGER NUMBER** — raising it would have made `sd_quote_requests` keyed on `lead_id`, which is **sd_crm's** id column on another table, because its own branch holds no `on_conflict` at all. The region is now bounded by the **next dispatch**, and grouping for `resource === 'a' \|\| resource === 'b'` is **same-line**, not "within 200 chars" — the first attempt used 200 and **merged two genuinely separate short branches, reintroducing the same over-reach one line below its own fix**, caught by new probe arm 11C. **Measured effect: UNRESOLVED 87 → 58, "UNRESOLVED with no removal verb" 60 → 30, single-row 2 → 3** — and that last one is the cleanest confirmation available, because the tool's header has always named THREE single-row collection upserts and the derivation had two of them plus a wrong one; **prose and derivation agree for the first time**. Four new probe arms hold both directions (11A far write still read, 11B a neighbour's single-row write not inherited, 11C no borrowing when a branch has no write of its own, 11D a shared dispatch still classifies both). **BURN-DOWN: THREE StoneDesk Tier A resources assessed from a read of their writers, 320 → 317 unassessed.** `sd_hr_certs` and `sd_hr_employees` are **NOT append-only** (both upserted in place) but deletion is forbidden — **OSHA 1910.1053(k)(3) requires the employer to MAKE AND MAINTAIN the silica training record**, `sql/sd_hr_schema.sql:84` grants select/insert/update only so there is no delete path to call, and `removeEmployee()` sets `status='Inactive'` rather than splicing the row out, which an earlier version did while telling the user it "cannot be undone". Same framing as `law_trusttx` — *append-only* would be FALSE of them, and forbidding deletion is the design. **`sd_quote_requests` came out the OTHER way and is recorded as a real gap rather than dressed as a design:** refusing to let staff EDIT the submitted text is an argument against editing, **not against removal**, and the two were being treated as one answer. **Declining does not hide it** — `pcRenderRequests()` renders every row with no status filter, so a declined request stays in the table permanently, and the feed is an unauthenticated public form, so the inbox grows monotonically and the shop cannot clear it. Whether the answer is a delete verb, a soft delete or a panel filter is a product decision and was not taken here. **DECIDED AND SHIPPED 2026-09-12 (Michael's call, CC implemented): SOFT DELETE PLUS A DEFAULT PANEL FILTER — and it is the first of these to be FIXED rather than given a reason, so `sd_quote_requests` LEAVES the queue. Removal verbs 50 → 51, stuck 320 → 319, and TIER A 54 → 53.** The verb is `soft_delete`, not `delete`, for the reason the platform decision already gives — the row stays and stays recoverable, the marker lives in the existing jsonb, and **no new database privilege is needed**, so `sql/stonedesk_public_surface_schema.sql`'s select/insert/update grant stays exactly as written. **THE SUBMITTED TEXT IS STILL NOT EDITABLE:** the handler does a **read-modify-write of the STORED record**, adding `_deleted_at` and `_deleted_by` and nothing else, so a delete cannot double as the edit path this resource refuses to have — the arm that sends a payload full of overwriting fields and asserts none of them land is the one most worth keeping. **The API is the boundary, not the panel:** a status change on a soft-deleted request answers **409 DELETED** and writes nothing, because "the UI does not show it" has never been an access rule here and promoting a deleted request would resurrect it in every count computed from status. **The panel now opens on what is WAITING, not on the archive** — promoted and declined are filtered out by default, **with the hidden count stated on screen**, because a filter that silently removes rows is the same class of thing as an empty state that is really a failed read. The flag is deliberately **not persisted**: a shop that ticked it once six weeks ago would silently be back to the unbounded list with no sign of why. **"Nothing waiting on you" and "No quote requests yet" are different sentences and stay different** — the 2026-09-04 false-empty fix is re-asserted rather than assumed to survive. **A FAILED DELETE LEAVES THE ROW ON SCREEN**: this panel has no local cache, so an optimistic removal would show a deletion that did not happen and the next load would bring it back unexplained. Held by `api/sd-data-quote-request-soft-delete.test.js` (14 arms, driving the REAL handler — 401/403 on every non-management role the app actually has, 404 vs **502 READ_FAILED saying the request is STILL THERE**, 503 NOT_PROVISIONED, already-deleted reported as itself with no second write) and `tests/quote_request_soft_delete_panel.js` (16 arms on the real panel functions, including a mutation that restores the unfiltered render and asserts the archive comes back, and a guard that the confirm text never claims "cannot be undone" — which would be false here). **One collateral repair:** `tests/public_catalog_no_false_empty.js` hand-declared the panel's IIFE variables in its own sandbox and threw `ReferenceError` on a correct file the moment `pcShowHandled` was added — a suite failing because its own copy of a declaration went stale, the same shape as an anchor that stops matching. It now takes that line from the real file, as it already did for `_sdAuthRefused`. **SECOND BURN-DOWN PASS 2026-09-12 (CC), same day: 321 → 318 stuck, removal verbs 50 → 52, and the second fix is the sharpest defect found in this whole exercise. 🚫 `sd_customers`: THE DELETION UNDID ITSELF AND THE USER WATCHED IT SUCCEED.** `custDelete()` filtered the record out of the local array and stopped there; `saveSD3Data()` writes the **survivors** through one row at a time, so the deleted customer's server row was never touched; and `sdHydrateCustomers()` **merges the server's rows back in BY ID** on the next load. The customer came back. The confirm said *"Delete this customer?"* with no caveat — which is the expensive part, because nobody had any reason to check. **AND IT REACHED A CUSTOMER:** `api/stonedesk-track.js` resolves a live **order-tracking link** against this table by `customer_id`, so in the window between the local delete and the resurrection a customer could still read their job status from a record the shop believed was gone. The same shape `api/_resources/sairndental.js` already records about `dnt_supplies`, and StoneDesk had it worse. **The READ filter is the half that makes a deletion stick and the client cannot supply it** — a record it has deleted is a record it no longer knows to skip, so only the query can. **THREE OUTCOMES, NOT TWO, because collapsing them forces a choice between a deletion that silently undoes itself and a delete button that stops working:** a confirmed delete removes it locally; **404/503 means there is no server row — and 503 is the LIVE path today, since `sd_customers` does not exist until the public-surface migration runs** — so the local removal is the whole deletion and sticks; anything else **keeps the record and says so**, because removing it locally is precisely what lets it return. `undefined` status is deliberately **not** a failure: `sdData()` returns null without calling anything when there is no licence, and treating never-called as failed would make an unlicensed install unable to delete. Held by `api/sd-data-customer-soft-delete.test.js` (10 arms) and `tests/customer_delete_does_not_resurrect.js` (14, including a **mutant that restores the pre-fix body and demands the record come back** — a resurrection test that has never seen a resurrection is asserting a property of its own fixture). **A THIRD TRANSPORT MAP WAS NEEDED AND ITS ONE LINE BROKE FIVE SUITES, every one of them on a CORRECT file.** `_sdLastStatus` records the HTTP status per resource (0 = never answered), because *which* could-not-ask it was is the fact the three-way decision needs. Five suites hand-list the transport's declarations in their own sandbox, so the real `sdData()` threw `ReferenceError` inside the vm and the catch turned that into a null return — every call silently "failing" for a reason about the sandbox. **Third time this week a hand-written mirror of a declaration has gone stale.** **`exec_context` ASSESSED AND IT IS A FALSE ENTRY:** read-only, **no table at all** — its own branch comment says *"There is no write action and no table — the module IS the store"*. **NOT fixed in the tool, deliberately, and the near-miss is worth more than the fix would have been:** a derived *read-only* classification needs to prove a resource never writes, and my first scan for exactly that called **FOURTEEN SAIRNdental resources read-only — including `dnt_patients`, `dnt_charges` and `dnt_payments`** — because they write through a generic map rather than a `resource === 'x'` branch. **A blind zero, and acting on it would have silently exempted three Tier A money resources**, the identical failure this row already records about the 2500-char window. Caught by spot-checking one name I did not believe, not by the count. **⚠ NEW, UNRESOLVED, AND IT MEANS THIS ROW'S HEADLINE NUMBER IS OPTIMISTIC: DECLARING A REMOVAL VERB IS NOT CALLING ONE.** `removal_path_check.py` counts a resource as having a removal path when `EXTRA_ACTIONS` declares one. Measured 2026-09-12 across every app HTML: **52 declare a verb, 30 have a client caller, 22 have none — and 21 of the 22 are StoneDesk.** For StoneDesk the zero is not a matcher artefact: the literal string `soft_delete` appears in `stonedesk.html` **exactly twice**, and both occurrences are the calls added the same day. So twenty-one verbs were wired into the API and nothing in the product ever invokes them — `sd_invoices`, `sd_photos`, `sd_comms`, `sd_fin_jobs`, `sd_templates` and sixteen more, every one with a local-only `*Delete()` that removes the row from the browser and leaves the server row behind. **That is the same class as the 15 hand-written cleanup SQL files this row exists to explain.** The 22nd is `sairncode`'s `sc_settings`, **not claimed** — that app may dispatch by variable and a bare zero there would be the blind-zero mistake again. **Not wired into the checker, because a naive caller-scan reproduces exactly that**; the measurement and its method are recorded here so the next pass starts from evidence rather than a fresh scan. **WIRED 2026-09-13 (CC) on Michael's decision — real capability, not dropped: `bc27f1fb`, `ab0a43fe`, `71ef8357`, live-verified.** **The 21 were the same defect as `sd_customers`, twenty-one times over:** `sdSyncCollection()` pushed **writes and nothing else**, so a row removed in a panel simply stopped being pushed and its server row was never touched — and `sdHydrateAll()` merges the server's rows back in **BY ID** and never deletes, so the record reappeared on the next load. The `soft_delete` branch and its `data->>_deleted_at=is.null` read filter had existed since 2026-09-08; **only the call was missing.** **DONE IN ONE PLACE, NOT TWENTY-ONE** — `sdSyncCollection()` is already the seam every write goes through, keyed by the same storage key, computing the same diff; twenty-one handler edits would have been the bulk find-replace CLAUDE.md forbids and would miss the twenty-second. **⚠ MY OWN CHANGE SHIPPED A REGRESSION AND I FOUND IT AN HOUR LATER BY ASKING WHY FIVE COLLECTIONS HAD NO DELETE BUTTON.** They have none because they are not curated lists — they are **capped logs**: drawings trim to 20, snapshots to 90, order history to 200, saved nests to 50, email threats to 100. **Those caps are localStorage QUOTA bounds, not retention policy** (`sd_drawings`' own comment says the 50→20 cut "costs history depth"), and the server has no such bound — it was quietly keeping the deeper archive. The sweep turned **every trim into a server-side deletion**, silently, on every save. **A diff cannot tell a cap from a deletion**, so the trimming site now says which: `sdCapLocal()` registers the dropped ids and the next sweep skips them, **consumed once** — a standing exemption would silence real deletions of that id for ever. Not `sdSyncSuppressed` at those sites, because that would also suppress the **write of the row just added**, which is the record the user is trying to back up. A derived arm fails if a **sixth** cap appears, proven to bite by reverting one site. **HONEST COVERAGE, because "wired" and "usable" are different claims: 19 of the 21 are arrays and the sweep carries their removals; 2 are OBJECTS — `sd_negotiated_prices` and `sd_pricing_rules` — and `sdSyncCollection()` returns early on a non-array, so those two have NEVER been backed up at all, writes or deletes, despite being listed in `SD_SYNCED`.** Of the 19, **nine have a confirmed user-facing delete path** (`invDeleteInvoice`, `remakeDelete`, `finDeleteJob`, `invDelete`, `fmDeleteStop`, `photoDelete`, `tmDeleteRecord`, `nestingRemove`, and **Saved Drawings, whose Delete button was added today** — until then the only way to lose a drawing was to push it off the 20-entry cap). **The remainder are append-only streams with no list UI to hang a button on** — SMS log, AI quotes, VeinMatch and SeamAI analyses, exec messages, email threats, business snapshots, order history — **and `stonedesk_quote_history` is rendered only by `renderHistory()`, which writes into `history-list`, an element the file's own comment says was never built.** Adding delete UI to those is a **product decision, not wiring**: several are plausibly audit trails that should stay append-only. **Also found and NOT fixed:** `commsDelete()` filters `sdCommsThreads`, which `saveSD5()` does not save and which the file already records as diverged from the `sd_comms` store — so that button has never persisted anything, before or after this change. **COMPLETED 2026-09-13 (CC) on Michael's decision — real delete UI for every remaining collection, not just wiring. Ten delete entry points live-verified on the deployed file.** Comms log, SMS log, VeinMatch, SeamAI, quote history, Quote Builder saves, exec channel, email threat log, KPI snapshots, vendor orders. **SIX OF THEM HAD NEVER BEEN BACKED UP EITHER, AND THE CAUSE WAS ONE LINE NOBODY HAD CONNECTED TO THEM:** `sdSyncCollection()` skips any row whose `id` is missing, and six collections were built before that seam existed and never set one — so `sd_comms`, `sd_sms_log`, `sd_veinmatch`, `sd_seamai`, `sd_email_threats` and `sd_business_snapshots` sat on a list whose name reads *"backed up"* while living entirely in one browser's cache. Back-filled through a shared `sdEnsureRowIds()`; **the id is DERIVED FROM THE ROW'S CONTENT, which is the load-bearing choice** — a random back-fill id differs per device, so one message would sync as one server row per browser that ever opened the panel and deleting it on one could not delete it on the other. **The FIELD LIST stays per-collection** and is the part a helper cannot decide: an arm pins that `msg` is in the SMS id, because two messages to the same person in the same minute with different text are different entries. **THREE COLLECTIONS HAD NO LIST AT ALL — a writer, a cap, and no reader.** VeinMatch and SeamAI wrote a row per analysis and showed only a COUNT of them; `sd_business_snapshots` had a writer, a 90-entry cap, a daily auto-save and the only reader was a *"last snapshot"* date used to decide whether to take another. **A count with no list behind it is a number nobody can check.** **AND THE APP HAS TWO "SAVE A QUOTE" BUTTONS WRITING TWO DIFFERENT STORES** — *Save to History* → `sd_quote_history` (displayed) and *Save Quote* → `stonedesk_quote_history` (rendered only by `renderHistory()` into `#history-list`, which the file's own comment records as never built). **Listed, NOT merged:** folding them into the table above would put them into Total Quotes, Total Value and Win Rate, silently moving four money figures every existing shop already reads, and an arm pins that `load()` still reads two stores so a later merge must be a decision rather than a line. **THE CAP GUARD FROM `ab0a43fe` HAD TWO HOLES AND BOTH WERE REAL:** it recognised only `slice(0,N)` and missed `sd_exec_msgs`' `slice(-500)`, and it attributed caps by PROXIMITY so it could not see past an aggregate saver — **proven by reverting the exec cap and watching the arm stay GREEN.** Rewritten to derive backing-variable → key from every `st(key,var)` site, which immediately found a **seventh** cap nobody had looked at: `sdPhotos.slice(0,200)`, saved by `saveSD3Data()`. **Two deliberate design calls worth naming:** the exec channel offers Delete on **your own messages only** and `execDelete()` re-checks the role rather than trusting the markup, because a button that is merely not drawn is not an access rule; and the vendor-order confirm says outright that **YTD spend and spend-by-vendor will drop**, because unlike every other log that one is SUMMED. **Held by `tests/comms_log_delete_and_ids.js`, `tests/sms_log_delete_and_ids.js`, `tests/ai_analysis_logs_delete.js`, `tests/quote_history_delete.js`, `tests/exec_chat_delete.js`, `tests/threat_and_snapshot_delete.js`, `tests/vendor_order_delete.js`, `tests/collection_delete_reaches_the_server.js`, `tests/customer_delete_does_not_resurrect.js` and `tests/stonedesk_saved_drawings.js`.** Also corrected before commit: I had written that `sd_order_history` was never backed up — it always set `id:'ORD'+Date.now()` and never failed the check, and an arm now asserts its back-fill writes nothing. **FOLLOW-UP 2026-09-13 (CC), `0f9dd05d` + `1a04284c`, both live-verified.** ① **The two caps raised as open were already closed in `ef04c0ee`** — `sd_exec_msgs` through `sdCapLocalTail()` and `sd_photos` through `sdCapLocal()`, both on origin and live; verified against the deployed file before touching anything rather than from memory. **What was genuinely unclosed was the coverage behind one of them:** `sdCapLocal()` had four behavioural arms and `sdCapLocalTail()` had ONE, source-level — that `execSend()` calls it. **Nothing had ever watched it exempt a row.** A helper with a source-level arm and no behavioural one is the same shape as a checker nobody has seen fail: it looks covered and is not, and the asymmetry with its own sibling is how that goes unnoticed. Four arms added, one specific to the variant — it asserts the cap keeps the **NEWEST** entries, because getting that backwards would silently discard the most recent 498 messages in the executive channel while every other assertion stayed green. Proven to bite. ② **🚫 THE LINE THAT HID SIX COLLECTIONS IS NOW LOUD, IN THE TWO APPS THAT WERE SILENT.** Every app's sync seam skips rows with no `id` — correct, there is nothing to key an upsert on — but **two of five did it silently**, so a collection that had never once reached the server looked exactly like one backed up on every save. **Measured across all five before changing anything, and the first pass was wrong in the permissive direction:** a keyword scan reported SAIRNbuild and SAIRNvet as having no id guard at all, and reading them showed both do. Another blind zero. Read, not scanned: **SAIRNfreedom and SAIRNvet already count and warn; SAIRNbiz back-fills instead so nothing is ever skipped; StoneDesk and SAIRNbuild (30 collections) did NEITHER** and now report, copied from `sfSyncCollection()` so four apps say the same thing about the same condition. **One line per collection per save, not one per row** — 400 idless rows would otherwise produce 400 identical warnings and get muted, which is its own way of saying nothing. **The last arm is the point of `tests/idless_rows_are_reported.js`: it DERIVES the set of apps carrying a `*SyncCollection` seam from the files and fails if it disagrees with its own table, so a sixth app cannot grow one and default to silence.** Assertions read a **comment-stripped** body, because every one of these functions now carries a paragraph explaining the warning and a check counting those would pass on a file whose code had lost the counter **SHARPENED 2026-09-13 (Fourth) with the witnessing-scope cross-reference, as a POINTER rather than a second row** &mdash; `docs/2026-09-13-irreversible-write-witnessing-scoping.md` calls this CLASS B and deliberately did NOT fold it into the lock, because doing so would have turned a scoped lock into a platform-wide rewrite on the strength of one word. **THE DISTINCTION IS THE USEFUL PART AND IT IS NOT A NICETY:** Class A is APPEND-ONLY BY DESIGN &mdash; a wrong row stands forever because a correction is a second row, which is the right shape for a regulated record and exactly why verification has to happen BEFORE the write. Class B is these 53: nobody DECIDED they are permanent, the product simply has no way to remove one. So the answers differ &mdash; Class A needs a witnessing lock, Class B needs a removal path, and a lock on Class B would be a gate in front of a door nobody meant to lock. `sv_controlled` sits in BOTH and is the sharpest single instance of either: Tier A, no removal path, and its own registry file calls it the DEA-relevant controlled-substance register. **Still unassigned, still standalone, and still a REVIEW QUEUE ORDERED BY CONSEQUENCE rather than 53 defects** &mdash; the burn-down says which matter most to fix and says nothing about whether any of them SHOULD become deletable. | M |

A probe passing off a comment is a check that has stopped checking. **The real repo is clean, and that is only worth saying because the probe ATTACKS the tool:** 5 assertions inspected, 4 comment-only and every one deliberate and declared &mdash; two assert a historical record SURVIVES, two use a heading comment as a block LOCATOR and assert the miss at `start > 0`. | **Platform** | **A GCM auth tag was accepted at any length Node allows, on both encrypt-at-rest paths** | **CLOSED 2026-09-10 (CC)** &mdash; `9139d626`, found by Semgrep `gcm-no-tag-length` | CC | &mdash; | `api/_lib/auth.js` `decryptSecret()` and `api/_lib/token-vault.js` `decrypt()` both called `createDecipheriv` **without `authTagLength`**. In that state Node accepts a GCM tag of **4, 8, or 12&ndash;16 bytes**, and both functions read the tag **straight out of the stored ciphertext** &mdash; so anything able to write that value could present a **four-byte tag and drop forgery resistance from 2^128 to 2^32**. **Nothing this codebase wrote is rejected:** both encrypt paths call `getAuthTag()` with no argument, which has always produced the full 16. The length is checked **before** `setAuthTag` as well as pinned in the constructor, so each file keeps its deliberately opposite failure convention &mdash; `decryptSecret()` returns `null` (it must never throw detail back to a caller), token-vault throws `BAD_FORMAT` (it must distinguish *tampered with* from *absent*). A short tag is a **format** problem, not a bad-tag problem, and now says so. **Verified live, not assumed:** round-trip still succeeds on both, and the same ciphertext with its tag truncated to 4 bytes is refused &mdash; token-vault `BAD_FORMAT "auth tag is 4 bytes, not 16"`, auth.js `null`. | S |

Same shape as Texas. **TWO JURISDICTIONS HAVE NOW ANSWERED IT THEMSELVES AND THEY ANSWER IT DIFFERENTLY, which is the strongest argument for asking this once rather than per state: WASHINGTON's CR 6(a) says outright "Legal holidays are prescribed in RCW 1.16.050" — an express cross-reference — and that statute then excludes its own decoys in subsection (7) ("may not be considered legal holidays for any purpose"); NORTH CAROLINA's Rule 6(a) instead asks whether "the courthouse is closed for transactions", so its statute is the wrong source entirely.** So the answer is not uniform and the question is really: which source does THIS rule's own words point at, and what do you do when they point at nothing? The common question: **when a court rule says "legal holiday" and points at nothing, does the general holiday statute supply the list, even where that statute is broader or narrower than what the courts actually observe?** Add the two Texas secondary-source rows to the same set while a lawyer is engaged **CATEGORY ADDED 2026-08-26, on Michael’s direction, covering MARYLAND and WISCONSIN together rather than as two new categories — they are the SAME SHAPE: a plausible-looking source that fails in the DANGEROUS direction.** Every jurisdiction above asks *which* list supplies “legal holiday”. These two ask something sharper: **the obvious source is not merely uncertain, it is affirmatively WRONG, and using it rolls deadlines LATE.** **(6) MARYLAND** — the intuitive path (Gen. Provisions § 1-302 + § 1-111) is wrong in BOTH directions at once: § 1-302 rolls only off Sunday, with no Saturday roll (→ EARLY), while § 1-111 adds Good Friday, Lincoln’s Birthday, Maryland Day and Defenders’ Day, four days that are NOT court holidays (→ LATE). Rule 1-203’s own committee note settles it — it **supersedes § 1-302**. Correct chain: Rule 1-203 → Rule 1-202(l) → **State Personnel & Pensions § 9-201**. **(7) WISCONSIN** — the wrongness is not which statute but **which TEST**. § 801.15(1)(b) rolls the last day unless it is “a day the clerk of courts office is closed” (a CLOSURE test), while the composed holiday definition in (1)(a) governs ONLY the sub-11-day intermediate-day exclusion. So the obvious move — drive the rollover off the holiday list — is the wrong basis, and because Wisconsin’s clerks of circuit court are COUNTY officers, any clerk open on a listed day means the rollover fires when the statute would not: **LATE**. The 1985 Law Revision Committee Note makes it worse rather than better, saying the amendment “will **permit** clerks to close their offices at these times” — permit, not require. **WHY THESE TWO BELONG WITH THE OTHERS AND NOT IN A ROW OF THEIR OWN:** the answer a lawyer gives to “when a rule says legal holiday and points at nothing, does the general statute supply the list?” is the same reasoning that answers “and what if the general statute is affirmatively the wrong one?” Splitting them would invite two inconsistent answers. **Both states are GATED-PASSED but deliberately UNSEEDED pending this** — see their own rows. Contrast the two that resolved safely: **MISSOURI**, where RSMo 9.010 is titled “Public holidays” (the identical lexical gap that helped kill Kentucky) but converges day-for-day with the state’s own schedule, so both readings agree; and **MASSACHUSETTS**, whose Rule 6(a) names its statute expressly. The distinction the lawyer needs to draw is CONVERGES vs DIVERGES, not NAMED vs UNNAMED. | L |

Observation shifts agree between the two lists (Sat→preceding Fri, Sun→succeeding Mon), and Arkansas’s is GENERAL rather than enumerated, unlike NV’s and UT’s. **SHORT-PERIOD EXCLUSION IS FOURTEEN DAYS — A NEW NUMBER AND THE LONGEST IN THE PLATFORM** (six states use 7, three use 11, MN/UT/NV have none). Lee’s Birthday, leaving “Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.’s Birthday — the third Monday in January”; § 5 moves Robert E. Lee Day to § 1-5-106 gubernatorial-proclamation memorial days (second Saturday in October), which is **NOT a holiday and must not enter a calendar**. **✅ PRIMARY 2 — THE TREASURER OF STATE’S SHEET** (`media.ark.org/artreasury/holidays_2025.pdf`, on the State’s own CDN): “2025 State Holidays — Legal holidays by authority of **Act 304 of 2001 and Amended by Act 561 of 2017**”, enumerating ten dated days that match Justia exactly and **independently confirming CHRISTMAS EVE**. Connecticut (~3.6M); rules of court are the **Practice Book**, adopted by the judges of the Superior Court. **SOURCES ARE AMONG THE CLEANEST GATED:** the Judicial Branch publishes the **OFFICIAL 2026 Practice Book** as one free PDF on plain curl — 3.6 MB, 699 pages, a **real text PDF not a scan**, first page reading “OFFICIAL / 2026 / CONNECTICUT PRACTICE BOOK” — with per-section amendment histories giving real `effective_from`; `cga.ct.gov` serves the General Statutes free too. Nothing here is the blocker. **BLOCKER ONE: SEC. 10-8 IS A CHAIN, NOT A DEADLINE.** Pleadings “shall advance within thirty days from the **return day**, and any subsequent pleadings … shall advance at least one step within each successive period of thirty days **from the preceding pleading** or the filing of the decision of the judicial authority thereon”. So the *n*th deadline depends on the *(n−1)*th ACTUAL FILING DATE, indefinitely. **Every seeded jurisdiction computes ONE date from ONE caller-supplied trigger.** Maryland’s chained discovery floor was logged as the highest-stakes shape found in any gate because ONE LIMB depended on another rule’s output; **Connecticut’s entire pleading cadence is that shape as the PRIMARY mechanism**. Seedable only as “30 days from the preceding pleading”, with a trigger named so nobody mistakes it for “30 days from the return day”, and a readme saying plainly that **Connecticut has no single answer deadline to compute**. Two domain-scoped variants ride the same sentence: **summary process 3 days, mortgage foreclosure 15 days**. And the **RETURN DAY is a Connecticut-specific concept fixed by Gen. Stat. § 52-48 (NOT read)** — it is a date stated in the writ, **not derivable from a service date**, so it must be caller-supplied and a seed must not silently equate the two. **BLOCKER TWO: THE ROLLOVER HAS NO HOLIDAY BASIS AT ALL.** Running the new standing weekend-coverage check, Connecticut fails the question’s premise: **“holiday” appears FIVE times in 699 pages and none of the five is definitional** (two are professional-conduct commentary on gifts, one is juvenile detention). Sec. 63-2 and Sec. 7-17 both roll on **“a day when the office of the clerk … is closed”**. Weekends therefore come out right by accident of fact (offices are shut), but **encoding Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-4’s list for the rollover would risk rolling LATE if a clerk’s office is in fact open on a listed day — the Wisconsin hazard**. Sec. 7-17 says offices close “during weeks which include a legal holiday” but **never says which days**. Correct basis is the **Judicial Branch’s published court-closure schedule**, making Connecticut ingest-not-derive alongside NC, NJ, MD and OK; plus a discretionary limb (closure authorized by the administrative judge “due to the existence of special circumstances”) that is unknowable → EARLY. **NO INTERMEDIATE-DAY EXCLUSION, STATED AFFIRMATIVELY:** Sec. 63-2 — “**Time shall be counted by calendar, not working, days.**” So the field is ABSENT, and unlike Minnesota (where it had to be inferred from a days-are-days rule) Connecticut says it outright. **NO SERVICE EXTENSION FOUND ANYWHERE IN THE PRACTICE BOOK** — zero hits for “days shall be added”, “shall be added to the prescribed” and “additional time after service”. All nineteen seeded jurisdictions have one. **Reported as an absence searched for, NOT as a conclusion**: the General Statutes were not searched, and that is the single most important remaining read, because assuming “no extension” wrongly computes EARLY on every mailed period. **AN E-FILING CUTOFF THAT MOVES THE FILING, NOT THE DEADLINE:** Sec. 7-17 deems a document e-filed **after 5 p.m.** (or at any time on a closed day) filed on the next business day — mechanically Missouri’s completion rule but applied to **filing** rather than service, so it does not change the DATE this engine reports, only that a filer has until 5 p.m. rather than midnight. Row note, not a mechanism. **ALSO NOT READ:** Gen. Stat. § 1-4; the discovery periods (Secs. 13-6, 13-9, 13-22/13-23, located but not read); and the Judicial Branch closure schedule itself. **UPDATE 2026-08-27 — PARTIALLY SEEDED, DELIBERATELY UNPROVISIONED (Hank).** The chain row is now live in `sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_connecticut.json` — ONE row, `ct-pb-10-8-advance-from-preceding-pleading`, trigger `filing_of_preceding_pleading` (named at length so it cannot be read as `return_day`), 30 calendar days forward, new standard `ct_pb_63_2` (`impl: frcp_6a`, **no** `short_period_exclusion_days`), `effective_from` **2014-01-01** from Sec. 10-8’s own amendment line. **NO `ct` CALENDAR WAS CREATED AND THAT IS THE HOLD:** `rollOff()` consults the calendar BEFORE it looks at the weekday, so Connecticut refuses `NOT_PROVISIONED` on **every** date, not just weekends — the Wisconsin hazard cannot be walked into. `api/_lib/deadline-connecticut.test.js` (26 assertions) asserts that on a **Tuesday** landing as well as a weekend one and **FAILS IF ANYONE LOADS A `ct` CALENDAR**. No `JURISDICTION_COVERAGE` entry — that text rides on SUCCESSFUL computations, so one would be dormant (Guardian 0d); it goes in with the calendar. **RE-VERIFYING THE GATE AGAINST THE PDF FOUND THREE THINGS IT MISSED, one of which cuts the other way:** **(1) §3a, the only LATE-direction exposure —** the counting rule Sec. 63-2 sits under **RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE**, and on de-hyphenated text `first day shall` occurs **exactly once in 699 pages**, there; `computation of time`, `computing any period`, `period of time prescribed` and `intermediate Saturdays` are **0 hits each**. There is NO trial-court counting rule. 63-2 arguably still reaches Superior Court (it governs “any documents … under these rules” and its own rollover names “the clerk of the **trial court**”) but that is not conclusive — and if it does not, the first-day convention is ASSUMED not sourced and computes **LATE**. Stat. § 52-48; the return day is NOT derivable from a service date); the summary-process **3-day** and foreclosure **15-day** variants (real and quoted — held on a DOMAIN decision, `DOMAIN_LABELS` knows only `civil-litigation` and `appellate`, not on any doubt about the text); discovery, appellate and backward rows. **WHICH ITEM BLOCKS WHAT:** §3a and the closure schedule block the CALENDAR; § 52-48 blocks only the return-day row; a General-Statutes service extension blocks **nothing seeded** (this row runs from a FILING). 479/479 deadline tests pass. **⛔ HARD BLOCK, RESTATED EXPLICITLY ON MICHAEL’S DIRECTION 2026-08-27: DO NOT ADD A CONNECTICUT CALENDAR UNTIL THE FIRST-DAY-CONVENTION SOURCING QUESTION IS ANSWERED — DOING SO WOULD SILENTLY COMPUTE LATE.** The question in one sentence: **does Practice Book Sec. 63-2 reach Superior Court pleadings, or only appeals?** It is the sole source for “the last day shall, and the first day shall not, be counted” and it sits under RULES OF APPELLATE PROCEDURE. **This is a SECOND, INDEPENDENT blocker from the Wisconsin/closure-schedule hazard, and the more dangerous of the two** — every other disclosed Connecticut gap fails EARLY; this one fails LATE. **Answering the closure-schedule question alone does NOT unblock the calendar**, and shipping one on that basis is the specific mistake being guarded against: it would look like the hazard had been handled while the first-day convention was still assumed. Oklahoma (~4.1M), statutory civil procedure (Oklahoma Pleading Code, Title 12). **OSCN — the Oklahoma State Courts Network — publishes Titles 12 and 25 free on plain curl** with per-section Historical Data, and its title indexes list every section with its CiteID, so navigation is mechanical rather than guesswork. **IT HAS LOUISIANA’S SHAPE:** 12 O.S. § 2006(A)(1) rolls the last day only if it is “a legal holiday as defined by Section 82.1 of Title 25 … or any other day when the office of the court clerk does not remain open” — **Saturday and Sunday are NOT named**, exactly the structure that blocked Louisiana one gate earlier. **ONE CLAUSE SAVES IT:** 25 O.S. § 82.1(A) opens “The designation and dates of holidays in Oklahoma shall be as follows: **Each Saturday, Sunday**, …” — both weekend days, statewide, no county qualification. So the rollover reaches them and **the engine’s `isWeekend()` is correct here**, by a different textual route than any common-law state. **RECORD THIS AS A PATTERN, NOT A ONE-OFF:** three states running have had the weekend INSIDE the holiday list rather than beside it — Louisiana (Sunday only, parish-scoped Saturday → **blocked**), Oregon (Sunday in the list but Saturday also named separately in the rule → safe), Oklahoma (both, statewide → safe). **The gate question is no longer “does the rule name Saturday and Sunday” but “if it doesn’t, does the holiday statute cover both, everywhere?”** **EXCLUSION IS ELEVEN DAYS** (with TN/AZ/WI/AL), **and SIX SECTIONS ARE EXPRESSLY CARVED OUT of it** — §§ 765, 990.3, 1148.4, 1148.5, 1148.5A and 1756 count every intermediate day regardless of length. An *enumerated* opt-out, narrower than Louisiana’s open-ended “expressly excluded” and Minnesota’s open-ended opt-in, but still something a standard-level flag cannot express. None is in a first civil batch so it is recordable rather than blocking — **but seeding one later without noticing would apply an exclusion the statute removes, computing LATE**. The clerk-closure limb sits in BOTH the rollover and the exclusion and is a **partial-closure** test (“does not remain open … until the regularly scheduled closing time”), same breadth as Oregon’s; additional to the list rather than a replacement, so EARLY. **THE CALENDAR IS NOT FULLY DERIVABLE, FOR TWO INDEPENDENT REASONS.** (a) **The Christmas rule is the most complex encountered anywhere** — Dec 25, plus “the day before **or** after Christmas if Christmas is not on a Saturday or Sunday”, plus “the Thursday and Friday before Christmas if Christmas is on a Saturday”, plus “the Monday and Tuesday after Christmas, if Christmas is on a Sunday” — two or three holidays depending on the weekday, and **the general both-ways shift expressly does NOT apply to Christmas**. The before-or-after choice is simply not in the statute. (b) **§ 82.1(B) requires the Governor to issue an Executive Order EACH YEAR** specifying the dates — the **New Jersey annual-order shape layered on a statute** — and it is the only thing that resolves the Christmas choice. So Oklahoma is **ingest-per-year**, joining NJ, NC and MD, and is the first to be so for a **single day inside an otherwise derivable list**. The presidential limb (“the Governor **may** issue an Executive Order”) is discretionary and ad hoc on top: EARLY. **DO NOT ENCODE JUNETEENTH ON 19 JUNE.** Oklahoma’s is 25 O.S. **§ 82.4**, “**the third Saturday in June**”, a separate section — and § 2006 defines legal holiday by reference to **§ 82.1 only**. Practically it changes nothing because the third Saturday is already a holiday under “Each Saturday”, so it is **functionally invisible to deadline computation** — but encoding a 19 June holiday by analogy to the ten other seeded states would add a non-holiday and compute **LATE**. Also **no Columbus/Indigenous Peoples Day at all** (as in Oregon), and **the day after Thanksgiving IS statutory** (as in SC, unlike MN where it is a branch option). **SERVICE: +3 for mail, THIRD-PARTY COMMERCIAL CARRIER and electronic means** — ninth distinct answer on electronic service and the only one naming commercial carrier as its own category — period-lengthening, not Alabama’s federal after-expiry order. **BUT § 2006(D)’s proviso is a different TRIGGER, not a different amount:** where a summons and petition are served by mail, the answer runs from **the date of RECEIPT, or if refused the date of REFUSAL**, and takes **no +3**. Own row, or a caller supplying a service date computes EARLY. **AND THE ANSWER PERIOD CARRIES A PLAINTIFF’S ELECTION THE ENGINE CANNOT SEE:** § 2012(A) gives 20 days, but (A)(4) lets “the party requesting a summons to be issued … **elect** to have the answer served within **thirty-five (35) days** in lieu of the twenty” — a fact about what the requesting party chose, the same shape as Louisiana art. 1001’s 21-vs-30. **Two rows with unmissable names; guessing 35 where 20 applies computes LATE.** A defendant’s reservation of time adds a further 20 days while waiving defences — unseeable, but it only ever extends, so EARLY. **NOT DETERMINED:** the discovery periods (§§ 3233, 3234, 3236 — same source, effort remaining not a source problem); whether any of the six carved-out sections belongs in a civil batch; the current year’s Executive Order; and **25 O.S. § 82.2**, whose title suggests it bears on acts performable on holidays — § 2006 points only at § 82.1, but § 82.2 must be read to confirm it does not widen the definition **✅ SEEDED 2026-08-28 (Hank) — 9 rules, `sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_oklahoma.json`, new standards `ok_12_2006` and `ok_12_2006_d`, calendar 2026–2031 from `tools/gen_ok_calendar.py`. `deadline-oklahoma.test.js` 51/51.** All three gate conditions met. **(1) THE TWO FACTS THE ENGINE CANNOT DERIVE ARE FOUR SEPARATE ROWS, never one with a default** — the plaintiff’s 20-vs-35 election under § 2012(A)(4), and § 2006(D)’s proviso, which on MAILED process changes the **TRIGGER** to **receipt or refusal** rather than the amount. Trigger names carry both facts (`..._20_day_election`, `receipt_or_refusal_of_mailed_...`), a bare `service_of_summons_and_petition` matches **nothing**, and the test asserts all four exist and that none carries the extension. Guessing 35 where 20 applies is **fifteen days LATE**. **(2) THE SIX CARVED-OUT SECTIONS ARE RECORDED** (§§ 765, 990.3, 1148.4, 1148.5, 1148.5A, 1756 are excluded from the 11-day exclusion); none is in this batch, and the test asserts **no seeded row is under 11 days** so none reaches it. **(3) THE CALENDAR OMITS ONE DAY A YEAR AND DISCLOSES IT.** § 82.1(A) gives “the day before **OR** after Christmas” without saying which, and § 82.1(B) makes the Governor’s annual Executive Order the only resolver. **THOSE ORDERS ARE REACHABLE AND UNREADABLE** — sos.ok.gov publishes them, identifiable by title (**EO 2026-26 AMENDED**, 15 July 2026, for calendar 2027), but each is a **single-page scanned image with zero extractable text** (`/ProcSet [/PDF /ImageI]`, one `/Im1 Do`). Reading it needs OCR, which this project does not treat as verbatim. **Omitting reports EARLY; guessing would be wrong in BOTH directions at once** — adding a non-holiday (LATE) while still missing the real one. Affected years 2026, 2028–2031; **2027 is clean** (Saturday Christmas → the Thursday and Friday before, determinate). **THRESHOLD IS ELEVEN, not seven** — the test cross-asserts Oregon’s 7 against Oklahoma’s 11 so neither can drift into the other. **NO JUNETEENTH** (§ 2006 points at § 82.1 alone; Oklahoma’s is the **third Saturday in June** under § 82.4, already a non-day), **NO COLUMBUS DAY**, and **§ 82.2 was READ** to confirm its commemorative days stay outside — all three asserted by the generator. **The day after Thanksgiving IS a statutory holiday.** § 3236 turned out to need a **`resolve: later_of`** nobody had flagged: “The thirty-day response period shall not commence until an answer to the petition is filed”, so the clock runs 30 days from the LATER of request-service and answer-filing — seeding it flat would compute EARLY. **§§ 3233/3234 have NO defendant floor** (four phrasings searched, zero hits). Extension is +3 for mail, **third-party commercial carrier** (unique to Oklahoma) and **electronic means**; e-mail is NOT named and does not qualify. **Both tests proven to catch their defects:** encoding the omitted 24 Dec 2026 fails 2 of 51 including the arithmetic case, and dropping 11 to 7 fails the cross-assertion | L |

Oregon (~4.3M). **THE COUNCIL WRINKLE, CHECKED FIRST AND CONFIRMED REAL:** the ORCP are **not promulgated by the Supreme Court**. The Council on Court Procedures drafts and promulgates them, the **Legislative Assembly may then amend or repeal**, and they take effect as law the following 1 January — a two-stage lifecycle visible in the rules’ own citation lines, which carry **two amending authorities** (“CCP 12/6/14” alongside “2015 c.212 §8”). No other seeded jurisdiction has this. **AND THE COUNCIL’S OWN SITE DISCLAIMS ITS COPY:** “the first link is **static and may not include the most recent Council amendments nor amendments by the Legislature**”. Its static file is labelled **“Effective January 1, 2020”**, its “Amendments Made By Oregon Legislature” section is **empty and pending**, and its own news page records **2024 promulgations** (Rules 1, 14, 39, 55 and a new Rule 35) the ORCP page does not reflect. **So do NOT use the Council copy as the rule text** — take it from `oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/SiteAssets/ORCP.html`, the whole ORCP in one ~1.1 MB HTML file, **curl 200**, which is what was read. Standing consequence: the Legislature’s file is the TEXT and the Council’s promulgation record is the **forward channel** showing what becomes law next 1 January; both must be checked, in that order — the two-channel shape Maryland has, reached for a completely different structural reason. **IT DOES NOT HAVE LOUISIANA’S PROBLEM, AND THE DRAFTING IS WHY.** ORCP 10 A rolls off **“a Saturday or a legal holiday, including Sunday”** — Saturday named SEPARATELY, Sunday folded INTO the holiday definition. So although ORS 187.010(1)(a) makes “Each Sunday” a legal holiday (the same statutory quirk Louisiana has), Oregon’s rule rolls Saturday in its own right, statewide, and **the engine’s `isWeekend()` is correct here**. Worth stating explicitly because the two statutes look superficially alike and Louisiana was blocked on exactly this. **ORCP 10 A EXPRESSLY ANSWERS THE MARYLAND OPEN DECISION:** the sub-7-day threshold applies to the period **“(without regard to section B of this rule)”** — section B being the service extension — so **the 7-day test is measured BEFORE the 3 days are added**. Maryland’s Rule 1-203 leaves that identical question unresolved and it is logged as ship-disclosed-do-not-guess. Oregon does not decide Maryland, but it proves the question is a known one, that a drafter saw it coming, and **which way that drafter resolved it** — **carry this into the Maryland decision row as persuasive material.** **OTHER FIELDS:** exclusion is **seven**; the holiday basis is an express cross-reference to **BOTH ORS 187.010 and 187.020** (most states name one); there is a public-office-closure limb **broader than any seen** — it fires when the office is closed “before the end of **or for all of** the normal work day”, so a **partial-day** closure counts — and it is ADDITIONAL to the rollover rather than a replacement, so EARLY; no backward provision; and **ORCP 10 A disapplies itself to time limitations governed by ORS 174.120**, which was NOT read and must be before seeding. **ORCP 10 B IS THE BROADEST SERVICE ENUMERATION YET** — **+3 for mail, e-mail, facsimile AND electronic service** (eighth distinct answer on electronic service), period-lengthening not Alabama’s federal after-expiry order, and **“Except for service of summons” is stated in the rule itself**, removing the single most repeated inference in this engine — every other seeded state required deducing the Rule 4/Rule 5 scope split. **ORS 187.010 HAS A SELF-REFERENTIAL TRAP:** the shift is both ways, but the Sunday limb reads “Each time a holiday, **other than Sunday**, … falls on Sunday” — **without that carve-out every Sunday would make the following Monday a holiday**, because Sunday is itself item (1)(a). A blanket Sunday-shift generator would produce **52 phantom Mondays a year**. Being both-ways it also spills across the year boundary, so compute a wider span than you emit. ORS 187.020 adds Governor-appointed days and presidential days **only when the Governor also appoints** — note the conjunctive: a presidential day alone is NOT an Oregon holiday. Ad hoc, EARLY. **NO COLUMBUS/INDIGENOUS PEOPLES DAY AT ALL**, unlike AL, SC, LA, MN, MO, NJ, VA and MA. **OREGON HAS NO WRITTEN INTERROGATORIES.** Searching the entire ORCP for “interrogator” returns **four hits, all jury interrogatories** under Rule 61 C. There is no discovery-interrogatory rule at all — **every other seeded state has an interrogatory row; Oregon must have none, and that is the law rather than unfinished work**, which the seed readme has to say or the absence reads as a gap. **PERIODS:** ORCP 7 C(2) — defendant must **“appear and defend within 30 days”** (that phrasing, not “file an answer”), or 30 days from the date stated in the summons if served by publication; ORCP 43 B production **30 days with a 45-day defendant floor**; ORCP 45 B admissions **30/45 with silence ADMITTING**, plus a mandatory capital-letters warning on the request itself, the same device Missouri’s R. 59.01(a)(1) uses. Both floors run from **service of the summons**, a caller-supplied date, so Oregon does NOT hit the Maryland chained-floor gap **✅ SEEDED 2026-08-28 (Hank) — 6 rules, `sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_oregon.json`, new standards `or_orcp_10` and `or_orcp_10_b`, calendar 2026–2031 from `tools/gen_or_calendar.py`. `deadline-oregon.test.js` 52/52.** All four gate conditions met: text taken from the **Legislature’s** file not the Council’s static copy (asserted — every row’s URL is `oregonlegislature.gov`); **NO interrogatory row**, asserted so its absence cannot be read as unfinished work; the Sunday shift applied **only to holidays other than Sunday**, asserted by count in both the generator and the test; and **ORS 174.120 read** — it is the STATUTORY computation rule, it counts the same way but has **NO short-period exclusion at all**, so a statutory Oregon row must not use `or_orcp_10`. Not reached by any seeded row. **“EXCEPT FOR SERVICE OF SUMMONS” IS IN THE RULE’S OWN WORDS**, so the two 7 C(2) rows carry no extension and nothing rests on the inference that was got wrong federally. **THE EXTENSION REACHES E-MAIL, FAX AND ELECTRONIC SERVICE** — the opposite of NV/WV/NY/federal; the test asserts Nevada still adds 0 for e-mail on the same date Oregon adds 3, so if either ever matches the other one is wrong. **BOTH DISCOVERY FLOORS ARE `resolve_periods`** with different counts per limb (30/45), verified to pick the **45-day limb from the EARLIER trigger date** — exactly the case a plain `later_of` gets wrong — and to refuse `INCOMPLETE_TRIGGERS` on a partial set. The two floors use **different summons triggers** (43 B(2) from the summons, 45 B from the summons AND complaint) and the test asserts they stay distinct. **Test proven to catch a defect before being trusted:** injecting a phantom Columbus Day fails 3 of 52, including the arithmetic case. **The ORCP 10 A “without regard to section B” finding still belongs in the Maryland decision row** as persuasive material on the identical open question | L |

The 50-entry cap is therefore not a bound that protects anything. And `sd_drawings` is **local-only**: it appears in no resource registry and no sync list, so the 64 KB `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` cap in `api/sd-data.js` is not in play. Both hypotheses were checked and both came back clean.<br><br>**THE DECISION, with measured options rather than opinions — all four numbers are quota cost per entry, worst case:** today PNG 640×480 = **133 KB**; JPEG q0.85 same size = **70 KB**; JPEG q0.70 = **49 KB**; PNG at half scale (320×240) = **58 KB**; JPEG q0.85 at half scale = **23.5 KB**. Lowering the 50-entry cap is the other lever and costs no fidelity. **Not changed, because every option trades something a customer sees** — JPEG blurs crisp line art, downscaling loses detail on a drawing an operator reads dimensions from, and a smaller cap silently shortens history. This row asked to measure before changing anything; the measurement was done first and the change followed.<br><br>**DECIDED AND SHIPPED 2026-09-04 (Michael's call): JPEG q0.70 at FULL resolution, plus the cap 50 → 20.** Downscaling was rejected deliberately — an operator reading a dimension off an old drawing is a **functional** risk, not a cosmetic one.<br><br>**THE VISUAL CHECK BEFORE SHIPPING CAUGHT WHAT THE ARITHMETIC COULD NOT, and it would have been a correctness regression.** `ct-canvas` is **transparent** — the pale field is CSS, not pixels — and JPEG has no alpha, so a bare `toDataURL('image/jpeg', 0.70)` **flattens it to BLACK**. Seen in the browser: the grid lines vanish entirely, dark grey on black, and the drawing comes back as something the rep never drew. Shipping on the numbers alone would have traded a size problem for a worse one. The snapshot is now composited onto the canvas's **own computed** background first, read from `getComputedStyle` rather than hardcoded, with a white fallback because falling back to *none* is the black field again.<br><br>**Result, measured on the deployed build by driving the real `sdDrawSave()`:** 68,186 chars → **29,123 chars** (0.43×), quota cost **133 KB → 57 KB** per entry, whole store **~6.5 MB → ~1.1 MB**. Side by side the edge colour-coding, the texture and the panel label are all legible, and the JPEG is if anything closer to what the rep sees on screen than the transparent PNG was. **The live origin was restored exactly** — `sd_drawings` removed again, 654,296 chars and 199 keys before and after. 15 assertions in `tests/stonedesk_drawing_snapshot_budget.js`, four mutations probed; the composite has one assertion per load-bearing part, because the fill must happen BEFORE the `drawImage` or it covers the drawing.<br><br>**~~FOUND WHILE HERE, NOT FIXED — `sd_drawings` is WRITTEN AND NEVER READ.~~ CLOSED the same day (Cody) in `726677f9` on Michael's decision to build the missing half rather than delete the feature.** A **Saved Drawings** list now sits on the Drawing Tool toolbar: each row shows the drawing's own snapshot, its name and date, and loads it back onto the canvas. **The decision that made it more than a list is a correctness one:** the store held a PICTURE and nothing else, so a "reload" could only have painted a raster onto a canvas whose model still described something else — shape, dimensions and cutouts would all be whatever was on screen, and the first recalculation would contradict the image. `sdDrawSave()` therefore also stores `dcSnapshotDrawingState()`, **the same snapshot the quote history already keeps**, and the loader is the same `dcLoadDrawingState()` with the same `schemaVersion` check — no second mechanism. **Entries saved before this are listed, greyed, and told why** ("saved before drawings kept their measurements"), because hiding them reads as data loss and enabling them would be a control that does nothing. | **Tooling** | ~~Push-gate check 6 (the credential scan) reported itself UNCHECKED every time a push lost a race with another clone~~ | **FIXED 2026-09-04 (CC)** &mdash; root cause read out of the reflog, not reasoned; held by `tests/push_gate/redaction_base_probe.py` | CC | &mdash; | git hands a PRE-PUSH hook the sha the **remote has right now**, which by definition can be a commit this clone has never fetched. `git log <that sha>..<tip>` exits **128 Invalid revision range**, check 6 turned that into a bare RuntimeError, and the fail-open handler printed *"this push is UNCHECKED for credentials"* &mdash; so the push shipped scanned by nothing. **With four clones pushing concurrently this is the ORDINARY case, not an edge one:** it fires every time you lose a race. Observed live while pushing the SAIRNbiz work, then confirmed from `git reflog show origin/main` &mdash; the hook was handed `55a408a5` while this clone's origin/main was still `ae89eea5`, and `55a408a5` arrived on the NEXT fetch, after that push. **The fix falls back to a base this clone actually holds** (`@{u}`, then `origin/main`), which WIDENS the range &mdash; it can include commits already on origin &mdash; so the scan does more work, never less, and cannot miss a commit being sent. Fetching from inside a pre-push hook was rejected: slow, surprising, and it would make the gate depend on the network it exists to keep secrets off. It **says out loud** when it used a fallback base, because a scan over a range that is not exactly what ships must not read as one that was. The failure message now carries **git's own stderr** &mdash; the version that said only "failed" is what cost the diagnosis. **The sibling checks 1/2/3 were NOT affected, checked rather than assumed:** they read the same base through `outgoing_files()`, whose `git()` helper returns `''` on a non-zero exit instead of raising, so they already fell through. That is correct BY ACCIDENT and one edit away from being undone &mdash; making `git()` raise would silence every check on a raced push **with no message at all**, strictly worse than what was just fixed. The probe asserts it so that edit fails loudly. **Third wrong implementation of this check, and the first to fail in the ordinary case** rather than a contrived one; all three were found by driving it and missed by reasoning about it. | S |

Every degradation ends in "allowed", so the worst case is yesterday's behaviour and never a refused real request — it reduces the amplification factor of the ordinary case and is not a defence against a determined distributed attacker. The map is bounded at 5000 addresses, because a limiter that can be made to exhaust an instance's memory is a denial of service wearing a fix's clothes; its own probe caught that the first version settled at 5001 by pruning before the insert. **AND THEN PRODUCTION SAID IT DOES NOT WORK, which is the part that matters.** Live: 40 concurrent junk-token requests returned 40x 401 and NOT ONE 429, against a limit of 20 in 60 seconds. ## What this index does NOT cover, stated so the gap is known

- **Per-app handoffs were not read line by line.** Rows come from
  `SAIRN-BACKLOG.md` (section-by-section), `SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK.md`, and work
  done in-session on 2026-08-23. There are ~40 handoff files; an item that
  exists **only** inside one and never reached the backlog is not here yet.
  That is the first thing to improve on the next rebuild.
- **Sizing is judgment, not estimation.** S/M/L is a rough shape, not a
  commitment.
- **Owners are observed, not assigned.** `unassigned` means no session has
  claimed it in the active-work log (`SAIRN-ACTIVE-WORK.md` at rebuild time;
  now the three per-session files) — not that it is unimportant. Rows
  owned by **Michael** need a decision or an access level a session does not
  have.
- **⚠️ rows carry a number or claim this rebuild could not confirm.** They say
  so in Next action.

## Keeping it alive

This file rots the moment it stops being updated, and a stale index is worse
than none — it makes work look handled when it is not.

1. **When you close something, move the row** to *Recently closed* with the
   commit SHA. Do not delete it silently.
2. **When you find something new, add a row** in the same action as logging it
   in `SAIRN-BACKLOG.md`. Two places, one action, or they diverge.
3. **Re-derive, don't trust.** Before a planning decision, spot-check the rows
   you are about to rely on. This rebuild found one stale backlog entry
   (SAIRNlaw trust disbursement, listed open, actually shipped) out of 26 —
   assume a similar rate next time.
4. **Do not renumber or restructure the backlog to match this file.** The
   backlog is the detailed record; this is the index over it.
